headline: The Missile Defense Agency has awarded Lockheed Martin a $211.4 million contract modification to build new Configuration 3 (C3) THAAD launchers for the United Arab Emirates (UAE) under a Foreign Military Sales (FMS) agreement. The move is intended to strengthen the UAE’s ballistic missile defense capability while allowing its THAAD launchers to be more widely dispersed across the country. The significance of Configuration 3 goes beyond simply adding more launchers. It is part of THAAD’s broader hardware and software modernization, bringing improvements to cybersecurity and Link 16 communications while enhancing the system’s ability to integrate with a wider range of sensors. This is particularly important for the UAE, where key targets, including air bases, ports, population centers, energy facilities, and logistics infrastructure, are spread across a relatively large area. Recent regional missile attacks have demonstrated that effective interception is only part of the equation. Maintaining sufficient interceptor reserves and the ability to sustain defensive operations through multiple attack waves are equally critical. With the growing threat from ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones across the Middle East, the UAE is moving toward a more dispersed, interconnected, and resilient air defense architecture.

headline: The extended deployment of USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) and reported supply problems appear to be tied in part to the loss of the Navy’s logistics hub in Bahrain early in the Iran war according to a report from the New York Times. Iranian missile and drone strikes heavily damaged the Naval Support Activity Bahrain, home of the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet, forcing the Navy to shift much of its regional logistics support to Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia, roughly 2,200 miles from the carrier forces operating in the Gulf of Oman. The island subsequently became an Iranian target, with two ballistic missiles launched toward Diego Garcia on March 20; one fell short and a Navy ship intercepted the other. That logistical disruption has coincided with an unusually demanding deployment for Lincoln. The carrier has been at sea for nearly nine months without a liberty call, while supporting combat operations and the blockade of Iranian ports. Lawmakers have raised concerns about reported shortages of basic supplies and deteriorating crew morale. The Navy is now replacing Lincoln with the forward deployed USS George Washington (CVN-73), which is already transiting toward the Middle East. Another carrier, George H.W. Bush, has also been operating in the region for months.

headline: RT by @sentdefender: An Italian Eurofighter assigned to NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission shot down a drone of unconfirmed, but likely Russian origin after it entered Latvian airspace Friday, according to NATO and Latvian authorities. Two Italian Eurofighters scrambled from Lithuania along with two Turkish F-16s from Estonia. One of the Italian jets identified and engaged the drone. Latvian forces are now searching for the wreckage near Rugāji, about 35 km from the Russian border, so the drone’s origin has not yet been established. The incident comes amid a growing number of drone incursions into Baltic airspace. Latvia says Ukrainian drones have entered the region several times this year, while officials also point to Russian electronic warfare as a possible factor causing Ukrainian systems to stray across borders. Before Friday's incident, Ukrainian forces had launched attacks against Russian ports near St. Petersburg. Russian authorities claimed to have intercepted 15 Ukrainian drones during those attacks. This is the third reported NATO interception of a drone in the Baltics in recent months, following a Romanian F-16 shootdown in Estonia in May and a French Rafale shootdown in Latvia in June.

headline: The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow construction of the White House’s $400 million ballroom to continue while it appeals a lower court ruling that halted the project, according to the Associated Press. The D.C. Circuit ruled 2-1 that Trump cannot proceed without congressional approval, finding that the president lacks unilateral authority to build the 90,000 square foot structure where the East Wing once stood. The administration argues the project is necessary for White House security, calling the injunction unlawful and warning that stopping construction would leave an active construction site that is harder to secure.
